claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance and microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating are governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale precipitates formed during thermal exposure.
The baseline material is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The controlled intervention is thermal aging at 800°C for 10 hours.
Thermal aging at 800°C for 10 hours will promote nanoscale precipitate formation.
Thermal aging at 800°C for 10 hours will stabilize nanoscale precipitates.
The comparison will use sliding wear tests at 700°C under constant load and sliding speed.
Nanoscale precipitates formed during thermal aging are the proposed structural mediator.
The nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitate-mediated obstruction of dislocation motion reduces plastic deformation.
The nanoscale precipitates enhance coating hardness.
Reduced plastic deformation and enhanced hardness improve wear resistance.
At 700°C, the thermally aged coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited coating tested under identical conditions.
At 700°C, the thermally aged coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the as-deposited coating tested under identical conditions.
The predictions apply near 700°C under moderate loads when precipitate stability is maintained.
Precipitate size and distribution may vary with alloy composition and aging parameters.
Variation in precipitate size and distribution may alter the magnitude of the wear-resistance improvement.
